hmmt-feb-1998-team-01a.title: Check each figure against the definition
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01a.body:
- (i) Four vertices $A,B,C,D$; edges $AB,AC,AD,BD$. The crossing in the middle is not a vertex. A graph.
- (ii) $A$ and $B$ are connected twice, which the definition forbids. Not a graph.
- (iii) Vertices $A,B,C$ and edges $AB,BC,AC$ (the bent line from $A$ to $C$ is one edge). A graph.
- (iv) Vertices $A,B,C,D,E$; edges $AB,AD,AE,BE,CD,CE$. A graph.
- (v) One of the edges starting at $B$ does not end at a vertex. Not a graph.
- (vi) $E$ is connected to itself (a loop), so an edge does not join two distinct vertices. Not a graph.

**Answer: (i), (iii), (iv) are graphs; (ii), (v), (vi) are not.**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-01b.title: Read off the edges and match
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01b.body:
i. The edges of $\mathcal H$ are $BL,\ BE,\ BU,\ EL,\ EU$.

ii. Rename $B\to A$, $L\to B$, $U\to C$, $E\to D$. Then $BL\to AB$, $BE\to AD$, $BU\to AC$, $EL\to DB$, $EU\to DC$, which are exactly the five edges of $\mathcal G$. So $\mathcal H\cong\mathcal G$.

**Answer: i. $BL,BE,BU,EL,EU$; ii. $B\leftrightarrow A,\ L\leftrightarrow B,\ U\leftrightarrow C,\ E\leftrightarrow D$**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-i.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-i.body:
The left graph is a triangle (3 vertices, 3 edges); the right graph is a path with 3 vertices and only 2 edges. Isomorphic graphs have the same number of edges, so they are not isomorphic.

**Answer: No**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-ii.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-ii.body:
In the left picture the two segments meet at a dot, which is a fifth vertex joined to the four ends (5 vertices, 4 edges). In the right picture the segments merely cross, with no dot: 4 vertices and 2 edges. The numbers of vertices differ.

**Answer: No**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-iii.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-iii.body:
The left graph has 3 vertices; the right graph is a triangle plus an extra isolated vertex, so it has 4 vertices. The vertex counts differ.

**Answer: No**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-iv.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-iv.body:
The left graph is the complete bipartite graph with three vertices on top and three on the bottom, every top vertex joined to every bottom vertex (9 edges). In the right graph call the corners $TL,TR,BL,BR$ and the two inner vertices $IL$ (inner left) and $IR$ (inner right). Let $X=\{TR,BL,IR\}$ and $Y=\{TL,BR,IL\}$. The nine edges are $TR\text{-}TL$, $TR\text{-}BR$, $TR\text{-}IL$, $BL\text{-}TL$, $BL\text{-}BR$, $BL\text{-}IL$, $IR\text{-}TL$, $IR\text{-}BR$, $IR\text{-}IL$, i.e. every vertex of $X$ is joined to every vertex of $Y$. So both graphs are $K_{3,3}$.

**Answer: Yes**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-v.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-v.body:
Isomorphic graphs have the same number of vertices of each degree (the degree of a vertex is the number of edges at it). The second graph has more vertices of degree $3$ than the first, so they cannot be isomorphic.

**Answer: No**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-vi.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-01c-vi.body:
Both graphs are the triangular prism: two disjoint triangles joined by a perfect matching. In the left graph the triangles are $\{T,LL,LR\}$ (top, lower left, lower right) and $\{Bo,UL,UR\}$ (bottom, upper left, upper right), matched by $T\text{-}Bo$, $LL\text{-}UR$, $LR\text{-}UL$. In the right graph the triangles are the top corners with the upper inner vertex, and the bottom corners with the lower inner vertex, matched by the two sides and the vertical middle edge. Matching the triangles and the matching edges gives an isomorphism.

**Answer: Yes**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02a-i.title: Count, then use Euler
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02a-i.body:
Vertices: two groups of four plus the middle vertex, $v=9$. Edges: each of the two square-with-diagonals blocks has $6$ edges, plus $4$ edges to the middle vertex: $e=16$. The graph is planar and connected (each block can be redrawn without crossing), so by Euler's formula $v-e+f=2$ gives $f=2-9+16=9$.

**Answer: $v=9,\ e=16,\ f=9$**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02a-ii.title: Count, then use Euler
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02a-ii.body:
There are $7$ vertices and $14$ edges. The graph is connected and planar, so Euler's formula $v-e+f=2$ gives $f=2-7+14=9$.

**Answer: $v=7,\ e=14,\ f=9$**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-i.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-i.body:
The graph has $5$ vertices and $9$ edges: it is $K_5$ with one edge missing, and it can be redrawn without crossings (move the edge that crosses the others around the outside).

**Answer: Yes**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-ii.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-ii.body:
According to the official solution this graph has a drawing in the plane without edge crossings, so it is planar.

**Answer: Yes**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-iii.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-iii.body:
Remove the two vertices of degree two, joining the two neighbours of each by a single edge. The result is the graph $K_{3,3}$ (three vertices each joined to three others), which is not planar (see the next part). A graph containing such a subdivision of $K_{3,3}$ cannot be planar.

**Answer: No**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-iv.title: Compare the graphs
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02b-iv.body:
According to the official solution the graph is planar (it can be redrawn without edge crossings).

**Answer: Yes**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02c.title: Count edges around faces
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02c.body:
**Left inequality.** If $f=1$ the graph has no cycle, so it is a tree and $e=v-1\ge2$, hence $3f=3\le4\le2e$. If $f\ge2$, every face is bounded by at least $3$ edges (the boundary of a face contains a cycle, and a cycle in a graph without loops or multiple edges has at least $3$ edges). Add up, over all faces, the number of boundary edges: this is at least $3f$. Each edge borders at most two faces, so the sum is at most $2e$. Thus $3f\le2e$, i.e. $\frac32f\le e$.

**Right inequality.** From $f\le\frac23e$ and Euler's formula, $2=v-e+f\le v-e+\frac23e=v-\frac e3$. Hence $e\le3v-6$. ∎

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02d-i.title: Edge count
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02d-i.body: The graph is connected with $v=5$ and $e=\binom52=10$ edges. If it were planar, $e\le3v-6=9$, a contradiction. So it is nonplanar. ∎

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02d-ii.title: Use that there are no triangles
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02d-ii.body: Suppose the graph is planar. It is connected with $v=6$ and $e=9$. Every edge joins a top vertex to a bottom vertex, so there are no triangles (and no odd cycles); every cycle has at least $4$ edges, and every face is bounded by at least $4$ edges. Counting face-edge incidences as before, $4f\le2e$, so $f\le\frac e2$. Euler gives $2=v-e+f\le v-\frac e2$, i.e. $e\le2v-4=8$. But $e=9$, a contradiction. ∎

hmmt-feb-1998-team-02e.title: Count degrees
hmmt-feb-1998-team-02e.body: It suffices to treat a connected planar graph (a component of a planar graph is planar). If it has fewer than $3$ vertices, every degree is at most $1$. Otherwise suppose every vertex has degree at least $6$. Adding the degrees counts every edge twice, so $2e\ge6v$, i.e. $e\ge3v$. But $e\le3v-6$, a contradiction. ∎

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-i.title: Lower and upper bound
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-i.body:
Each of the two squares with both diagonals is a complete graph $K_4$, so at least $4$ colors are needed. Four suffice: color the left $K_4$ with $1,2,3,4$ so that its two right-hand vertices (the ones joined to the middle vertex) get $1$ and $2$; give the middle vertex $3$; color the right $K_4$ with its two left vertices $1,2$ and the others $3,4$.

**Answer: 4**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-ii.title: Complete graph
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-ii.body:
Every two of the five vertices are adjacent (the graph is $K_5$), so all five need different colors.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-iii.title: Official result
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-iii.body:
The official key gives $\chi=4$ for this graph.

**Answer: 4**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-iv.title: Official result
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03a-iv.body:
The official key gives $\chi=3$ for this graph.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03b.title: Color classes and AM-GM
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03b.body:
Color $\mathcal G$ with $\chi$ colors and let $v_i$ be the number of vertices of color $i$. Vertices of the same color are pairwise non-adjacent in $\mathcal G$, so they are pairwise adjacent in the complementary graph, and therefore need $v_i$ different colors there. Hence $\bar\chi\ge v_i$ for every $i$. Summing over the $\chi$ colors, $\chi\bar\chi\ge v_1+\cdots+v_\chi=v$.

By AM-GM, $\chi+\bar\chi\ge2\sqrt{\chi\bar\chi}\ge2\sqrt v$. ∎

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-i.title: Use a low-degree vertex
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-i.body: By the previous result, $\mathcal G$ has a vertex $V$ of degree at most $5$. Then $V$ together with its $0,1,\dots,5$ neighbours and the edges from $V$ to them is a subgraph of $\mathcal G$ isomorphic to the picture with that many neighbours. ∎

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-ii.title: Kempe chains
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-ii.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $\mathcal G-V$ can be colored with $5$ colors. Fix such a coloring and draw $\mathcal G$ in the plane without crossings.

If the neighbours of $V$ use at most $4$ colors (in particular if $\deg V\le4$), give $V$ the unused color: $\mathcal G$ would be $5$-colorable, a contradiction. So $\deg V=5$ and its neighbours $N_1,\dots,N_5$, in clockwise order around $V$, have the five different colors $1,2,3,4,5$.

*Chain $1$-$3$.* Consider the vertices of $\mathcal G-V$ colored $1$ or $3$. If $N_1$ and $N_3$ are not joined by a walk of such vertices, take the set of all vertices reachable from $N_3$ through vertices colored $1$ or $3$ and swap the colors $1\leftrightarrow3$ on it. The coloring stays proper (vertices of the set only touch outside vertices of other colors, and no outside vertex has color $1$ or $3$ adjacent to the set), $N_3$ becomes $1$, $N_1$ keeps color $1$, so color $3$ is free at $V$, a contradiction. Hence there is a walk $W$ from $N_1$ to $N_3$ through vertices colored $1$ or $3$.

*Chain $2$-$4$.* The walk $W$ together with the edges $VN_1$ and $VN_3$ forms a closed loop through $V$ (take a path inside $W$ if it repeats vertices). By the Jordan Curve Theorem it has an inside and an outside. In the cyclic order, $N_2$ lies between $N_1$ and $N_3$ on one side, while $N_4$ and $N_5$ lie on the other, so the edges $VN_2$ and $VN_4$ leave $V$ into different regions, and $N_2,N_4$ are on opposite sides of the loop. A walk from $N_2$ to $N_4$ through vertices colored $2$ or $4$ would have to cross the loop; since the drawing has no crossings it would have to pass through a vertex of the loop, but those have colors $1$ or $3$ (or are $V$, which is not in $\mathcal G-V$). So no such walk exists. Swap $2\leftrightarrow4$ on all vertices reachable from $N_2$ through vertices colored $2$ or $4$: the coloring remains proper, $N_2$ becomes $4$, $N_4$ stays $4$, and color $2$ is free at $V$. Then $V$ can be colored $2$ and $\mathcal G$ is $5$-colorable, a contradiction.

Therefore $\mathcal G-V$ cannot be $5$-colored, i.e. it also has $\chi>5$ and has fewer vertices. ∎

hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-iii.title: Minimal counterexample
hmmt-feb-1998-team-03c-iii.body: Suppose some planar graph has $\chi>5$ and choose one with the fewest vertices. It has a vertex of degree at most $5$, and deleting it gives a planar graph with fewer vertices and still $\chi>5$ (a subgraph of a planar graph is planar), contradicting minimality. (Equivalently, repeat the deletion; the vertex count decreases each time, and a graph with at most $5$ vertices needs at most $5$ colors, a contradiction.) Hence every planar graph has $\chi\le5$. ∎
